name: Merchant's House Museum (Seabury Tredwell House)

location.text: 29 East Fourth Street, Manhattan, New York

dates.altered: The 1930s survey records the house as 'Excellent. Hestored and now being used as a Museum'; the deed history it prints runs from Brewster's sale to Seabury Tredwell in 1835 to the 1935 conveyance to the Historic Landmark Society.
dates.note: Three dates on the record and none is edited. The survey's own form prints 'Date of Erection: 1831'; the Wikipedia infobox prints 'Built 1832'; the node's exemplar says 1832 and its note says 'Built 1831-32 by Joseph Brewster'.

refs.note: Read from the infobox summary returned by the search, not from the National Register's own database, which was not opened for this building.

refs.title: Merchant's House Museum - Wikipedia
refs.note: Its text: 'Built by the hatter Joseph Brewster in 1831 and 1832, the edifice is a four-story building with a Federal-style brick facade and a Greek Revival interior' and 'The current museum was built as one of six identical houses on the same block.' The four-storey reading disagrees with the survey's three; both are kept.

refs.title: Save The Merchant's House Museum
refs.note: Its text: 'The house was built on speculation in 1832 by a hatter called Joseph Brewster. He sold it three years later in 1835 for $18,000 to Seabury Tredwell' -- the same 1835 price the survey's deed abstract prints.

measurements.name: storey_count
measurements.note: '■Hires' is OCR for 'Three'; read as three storeys over a basement and cellar, with an attic. A reading, marked as one -- and it disagrees with Wikipedia's 'four-story building', which is recorded in the refs and not reconciled here.

note: Written 5 Sep 2026 for Tranche 2. The survey is a 1930s one-form entry plus a deed abstract: it states materials and storeys and no dimension at all, which is why no width or depth is recorded. Worth carrying for the node: the surveyor calls the exterior walls brick and the roof slate and says nothing whatever about the Grecian interior the node names this house for -- the Lafever-derived joinery and the fourteen-foot double parlours are the museum's account and this corpus's, not the surveyor's.
